sources.title: Ryan Gosling’s Zero-G Stunts on ‘Project Hail Mary’ Broken Down by the Space Epic’s VFX Supervisors

discussion.body: The vomit comet pitch is the giveaway about priorities. Real weightlessness existed, on a plane, for seconds at a time, and somebody still decided the set was the part not worth giving up. So the actor stays anchored and the floating gets moved into post.

Maybe, but look at what the fix actually is: no digital double, just a real body plus drifting props. What sells zero-G on screen is the behaviour of the objects around a person, which is a physical logic the harness cannot fake by itself.

items.title: Faking Zero Gravity Without the Vomit Comet in ‘Project Hail Mary’
items.body:
The visual effects supervisor Paul Lambert called creating convincing zero gravity the most daunting of the huge challenges in the Ryan Gosling space epic ‘Project Hail Mary’. The crew pushed hard to shoot on the ‘vomit comet’, the aircraft manoeuvres that buy brief stretches of weightlessness, but the spacecraft sets were too elaborate to rebuild inside a plane. So Gosling performed on wire rigs, including a rotating harness.

Hanging, though, is not floating. When a suspended body still read as hanging rather than drifting, artists repositioned his legs, arms or torso and added objects that drifted through the frame. Weightlessness was built twice: once by the rig on set, and again by everything allowed to move around the body.

sources.title: ‘Our river is almost dead’: What’s killing an iconic Miramichi fishery?

discussion.body: This is a disagreement about what a river can be trusted to say. Curtis has watched two curves move together for years; the department wants a mechanism it can measure before it calls one of those curves a cause.
The caution cuts both ways though. Waiting for proof while a population slides is also a decision, and it is one that leaves the burden on the people whose working lives supply the counting.

items.title: A River With 500,000 Bass and Fewer Than 5,000 Returning Salmon
items.body:
On the Miramichi, the striped bass population is now north of 500,000 — some estimates run much higher — while salmon returns were below 5,000 in 2025, according to Department of Fisheries and Oceans numbers. The people who fish the river read those two figures as one story. Brock Curtis, who runs an outfitter store in Blackville, says the cause and effect are clear: “Our numbers are dropping as the bass numbers are increasing, and there's a direct correlation there.”

The department's own website is more guarded. Bass eat “variable numbers” of smolts each year, it says, and “it is not clear whether this natural predator-prey dynamic is limiting the number of returning adult salmon to the Miramichi river.” The counts are not in dispute. The causal claim is.

sources.title: Turning the tides: Could hidden sea power energise our coastal towns?

discussion.body: Thirty homes is a rounding error against a national grid, and a whole village's worth of supply if the machine is standing in your own water. The bet is on small being enough.

Small machines still have to survive the market that killed the big ones. The Pelamis P2, the first deep-water floating wave machine to put power into the national grid, was 180 metres long, widely admired, and in administration by 2014. Elegance has not been the scarce resource in marine energy.

items.title: The Tidal Turbine That Began With a Cord Across a Highland River
items.body:
In a fast-flowing river in the Scottish Highlands, the engineer David Mummery tied a length of cord tightly across the water, swam out, gripped it, and sank his head below the surface to let the current rush over him. That was more than a decade ago, and the point was not measurement but feel — how water behaves around a body in it.

The idea that came out of those swims became the Swimmer Turbine, a 50kW tidal generator named after the experience. Anchored to the seafloor, the fiberglass and steel device sits invisible below the surface and can generate enough electricity to power about 30 homes.

sources.title: Porn showing choking or incest to be banned from early November, government says

discussion.body: Possession is an offence here, not only production. The compliance line — delete what you have, stop sharing it — puts the expected change in behaviour in the audience, not just in the studios and platforms that make and host the material.

A possession offence makes viewers potential defendants. The review's worry was normalisation: what young people come to expect from sex. Whether a criminal statute changes that expectation, or only relocates the material, is the part nobody can currently demonstrate.

items.title: From 6 November, Porn Depicting Strangulation or Incest Is Criminal to Possess in England and Wales
items.body:
Online pornography depicting strangulation or incestuous relationships will be banned from early November, the government has announced. From 6 November, it will be illegal in England and Wales to possess or publish porn that shows strangulation or suffocation, depicts sexual activity between people who are related, or shows adults role-playing as children under 16.

The change hinges on a gap: non-fatal strangulation is already an offence when it happens without consent, but its depiction online has not been illegal. The rules follow a 2025 review of porn regulation, which found depictions of choking were “rife” on popular porn sites and had helped normalise the act among young people.

sources.title: With an ad aimed at Trump, this Republican exposed GOP angst about Latino voters

discussion.body: The 'back stabber' repost is the loudest thing here, but the quieter complaint may be the more instructive one. A voter in the district who says he'll cast a straight Democratic ballot calls Salazar's recent push against Trump's aggressive deportations too little, too late — a grievance about timing rather than policy.

Careful with the 57-31. It's a survey of registered voters who identify as Hispanic or Latino, a broad category, not a poll of Florida's 27th. A district can land well away from a category-wide generic ballot, and an incumbent with a challenger's name recognition problem is not the same as a party's national standing.

Fair — but the category is the point in a seat that is more than 70% Latino. If the erosion is real at that scale, it doesn't need to show up everywhere at once; it only needs to show up in a handful of seats like this one.

items.title: Trump Shared a 'Back Stabber' Post About Salazar. Her District Is More Than 70% Latino.
items.body: Salazar, whose Democratic challenger is former broadcast journalist Eliott Rodriguez, is defending a Miami-Dade County seat that is more than 70% Latino — the kind of electorate Republicans' 2024 wins relied heavily on, and the kind that has been drifting. A recent Equis Research survey of registered voters who identify as Hispanic or Latino found that if the election for Congress were held at that point, they would pick the Democratic candidate over the Republican by 57 to 31. Against that backdrop, a public rebuke from the top of the ticket stands out: Trump hit back at Salazar after her ad, sharing a post on TruthSocial in which another user called her a 'back stabber.'

sources.title: Montreal borough tightens rules on e-scooters as youth injuries skyrocket

discussion.body: The bylaw governs parks, trails and sidewalks. It leaves untouched the rules that decide who can ride where it counts: the provincial pilot lets anyone 14 and older use the devices on roads with speed limits under 50 km/h and on bike paths, with helmets required at all times.

A municipal bylaw is also the smallest available lever, and the trauma director's own list reaches past the borough: she points at manufacturers' labelling and at devices marketed as though they were toys, and says more needs to be done at the provincial and federal levels.

That distinction — vehicle or toy — is the one worth arguing about, and the injury profile is the argument. Close to 20 per cent of the cases require hospitalization, and Friedman's summary is blunt: these are not little cuts and bruises.

items.title: A Montreal Borough Bans E-Scooters From Its Parks, Trails and Sidewalks
items.body: The Montreal borough of Saint-Laurent has adopted a bylaw banning electric scooters and other motorized personal mobility devices in public areas that fall within its jurisdiction — city parks, trails and sidewalks. Councillor Vana Nazarian says the bylaw followed a series of incidents and near misses over the summer, as the popularity of the devices keeps growing. The trauma data explains the appetite for a ban. Deborah Friedman, the trauma director at the Montreal Children's Hospital, says traumatic injuries related to e-scooters are now 14 times the number seen in 2023, when the rules were first introduced.

sources.title: Major fire breaks out in Alberta after deadly incident at military base

discussion.body: The medical scale is the part that is hardest to absorb. An emergency department physician in Edmonton said this number of patients would overwhelm the city, and called it a one-in-every-15-to-25-year disaster.

Which is exactly why the unresolved parts should be left unresolved. The RCMP are investigating, the minister calls the situation active and delicate, and authorities were still working to determine what happened and expecting to say more.

items.title: A Fire at CFB Wainwright Killed and Injured People. By 11 p.m. It Was Being Held.
items.body: Canada's defense minister said people were killed and injured in an incident at a military base in Alberta that caused a major fire, and reports said large numbers of injured people were being transported to hospitals. Fire crews scrambled late into the night as fierce winds whipped flames beyond Canadian Forces Base Wainwright and into the surrounding rural area. By 11 p.m., the Municipal District of Wainwright said on social media that the fire was being held and that property and critical infrastructure were protected. Defense Minister David McGuinty said the RCMP were involved in investigating the incident and described the situation as 'very, very active and delicate.'
